title: Episode 103: The 231 MPH Wind on Mount Washington: The Greatest Gust on Earth
description:
On April 12, 1934, three young meteorologists hunkered inside a wooden observatory atop New Hampshire's Mount Washington measured an astonishing surface wind gust of 231 miles per hour—the fastest surface wind ever recorded on planet Earth for over six decades.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we ascend into the treacherous, sub-arctic crags of New Hampshire's Presidential Range to witness one of the most astonishing meteorological events in planetary history: the recorded two-hundred-and-thirty-one-mile-per-hour wind gust atop Mount Washington on April twelfth, nineteen thirty-four. Standing at six thousand two hundred and eighty-eight feet, Mount Washington is widely renowned as the 'Home of the World's Worst Weather,' situated at the convergence point of three major continental storm tracks. On a wild, ice-choked spring afternoon, three young meteorologists huddled inside a wooden shack chained to the bedrock, wielding wooden clubs to smash rime ice from a custom-engineered heated anemometer. What they recorded shook the scientific world and stood as an unbroken world record for sixty-two years. Here is George with the full, roaring account.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE HOME OF THE WORLD'S WORST WEATHER
Rising majestically above the White Mountains of northern New Hampshire, Mount Washington stands at an elevation of six thousand two hundred and eighty-eight feet. While modest in height compared to the fourteen-thousand-foot giants of the American Rockies or the Himalayas, Mount Washington occupies a geographical location that produces some of the most ferocious, erratic, and extreme weather anywhere on planet Earth. It sits at the exact meteorological crossroads of three primary continental storm tracks: cold polar air sweeping southward from Hudson Bay, low-pressure moisture surging northward from the Atlantic Gulf Stream, and temperate weather systems tracking eastward across the Great Lakes.
Furthermore, the mountain's topography forms a natural funnel. The steep, glacial valleys of Tuckerman Ravine, Huntington Ravine, and Crawford Notch act as colossal thermodynamic nozzles, compressing air masses and forcing them upward over the exposed summit ridge at terrifying velocities—a phenomenon known to atmospheric scientists as the Venturi effect. Hurricane-force winds exceeding seventy-four miles per hour occur on the summit on average more than one hundred days every year, accompanied by sub-zero temperatures and blinding rime-ice fogs that coat every exposed rock in thick, razor-sharp crystals.
Since the nineteenth century, when early climbers perished from hypothermia in sudden midsummer blizzards, the mountain has claimed over one hundred and sixty lives. Yet its terrifying atmosphere also made it an incomparable natural laboratory for atmospheric research, attracting daring scientists who sought to understand the mechanics of extreme weather. Native Abenaki tradition regarded the granite summit of Agiocochook as the sacred, forbidden dwelling place of the Great Spirit, warning that mortals who dared ascend into the clouds would face divine fury.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE GREAT DEPRESSION AND THE MOUNT WASHINGTON OBSERVATORY
In the autumn of nineteen thirty-two, at the lowest depth of the Great Depression, a small group of passionate young meteorologists resolved to establish a permanent year-round weather observatory atop the summit. Leading the audacious endeavor was twenty-four-year-old Salvatore Pagliuca, an Italian immigrant and brilliant electrical engineer; Wendell Lees, an experienced winter mountaineer; and twenty-two-year-old Alexander McKenzie, a talented radio technician. Operating with virtually no state funding, they relied on private donations, salvaged lumber, and equipment loaned by the Blue Hill Meteorological Observatory in Massachusetts.
For their winter headquarters, they occupied a rugged, low-slung wooden building known as the Stage Office, situated beside the mountain's historic cog railway terminus. Knowing that winter gales routinely tore wooden structures from their foundations, the young men reinforced the building with heavy timbers and bolted thick steel logging chains across the roof, anchoring the cables directly into the solid granite bedrock of the summit with heavy iron eyebolts.
Inside, the men lived in spartan, close quarters. Heat was provided by a coal-burning potbelly stove, and communication with the outside world was maintained via amateur radio transmitters operated by McKenzie. To record wind velocity, they mounted a special three-cup anemometer outside, but quickly discovered that normal instruments were useless: heavy rime ice accumulated on the spinning cups within minutes, freezing the mechanism solid and threatening to tear it from its mast. The young scientists weathered the howling polar gales with high spirits and fierce determination, keeping meticulous handwritten weather logs by the flickering amber glow of kerosene lanterns.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE GENESIS OF THE SUPER-ANEMOMETER
To overcome the lethal rime-ice problem, the observatory turned to master meteorological instrument designer Charles F. Marvin and Fergusson-type anemometers modified by the Blue Hill Observatory. The instrument, affectionately known as the 'Mount Washington anemometer,' was a triumph of mechanical engineering. It featured three heavy, hemispherical brass cups mounted on an ultra-lightweight, high-tensile steel spindle, carefully balanced on sapphire jewel bearings to minimize friction at high rotational speeds.
Crucially, the entire assembly was equipped with an internal electrical heating element designed to melt freezing rime ice before it could accumulate on the moving parts. The rotating cups closed an electrical circuit with every sixty revolutions, transmitting an electrical pulse via insulated wires down into the warmth of the observatory cabin. Inside, the pulses were recorded on a precision mechanical chronograph—a revolving paper drum driven by clockwork, where an ink pen drew a continuous trace across calibrated graph paper.
By counting the number of electrical ticks recorded within a measured sixty-second or ten-second interval, the meteorologists could calculate the exact wind velocity with mathematical precision. Prior to deployment, the instrument was extensively tested and calibrated in the high-speed wind tunnels of the Guggenheim Aeronautical Laboratory in Massachusetts, certified accurate up to velocities of two hundred and fifty miles per hour. Every delicate component of the Fergusson-type anemometer was crafted by hand in precision workshops, balancing microscopic tolerances against the crushing aerodynamic pressures of hurricane-force winds.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE STORM OF APRIL 11–12, 1934
On Wednesday, April eleventh, nineteen thirty-four, an extraordinary meteorological monster began taking shape along the Atlantic seaboard. A deep low-pressure system off the coast of North Carolina began intensifying rapidly, tracking northward while pulling in vast reserves of moist tropical air. Simultaneously, an intense high-pressure ridge parked over maritime Canada began driving bone-chilling sub-arctic air southward through Maine and New Hampshire. The two colossal air masses collided directly over the Presidential Range.
By midnight on April eleventh, summit winds began to howl with unnatural ferocity, exceeding one hundred miles per hour. Rime ice accumulated at an astonishing rate of three inches per hour, encasing the summit buildings in a surreal, white crystalline armor. By early morning on Thursday, April twelfth, the barometric pressure plunged to twenty-eight point five inches of mercury, and winds reached sustained speeds of one hundred and fifty miles per hour.
Inside the chained Stage Office, the noise was deafening. The building shuddered violently in its steel chain harness, the floor buckled, and walls groaned as millions of pounds of atmospheric pressure hammered against the wooden siding. The roar of the wind resembled the continuous, shrieking scream of a dozen freight trains passing inches overhead. Conversation inside the cabin was impossible without shouting directly into an ear. Super-cooled cloud droplets suspended in the moving air instantly froze upon contact with the wooden siding, encasing the entire mountaintop complex in a surreal, sculptured shell of razor-sharp white ice.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GREAT GUST: 231 MILES PER HOUR
As the afternoon progressed on April twelfth, conditions deteriorated into an unprecedented meteorological maelstrom. Despite the internal heating coils, the super-cooled fog began overwhelming the anemometer, depositing rime ice on the leading edges of the brass cups. Every fifteen to twenty minutes, one of the meteorologists—bundled in heavy wool coats, fleece-lined aviator helmets, and goggles—had to venture outside onto the catwalk with a heavy wooden club, battling sixty-mile-per-hour crosswinds in the shelter of the doorway to reach the mast and smash the ice from the spinning rotor before ducking back inside.
At twelve o'clock noon, the wind reached one hundred and eighty miles per hour. At one o'clock, sustained gales hovered above two hundred miles per hour. Then, at precisely one twenty-one on the afternoon of April twelfth, nineteen thirty-four, the ultimate gust struck. Outside, the atmospheric funnel unleashed a wall of moving air of unfathomable power. Inside, the three young scientists watched in stunned silence as the chronograph pen began frantically leaping across the rotating paper drum, ticking off electrical pulses with the speed of an automatic machine gun.
Alexander McKenzie and Salvatore Pagliuca leaned over the drum with a precision stopwatch, counting the electrical pulses over multiple intervals. When they calculated the velocity against their calibration tables, they stared at the figures in utter disbelief: over a five-second interval, the wind had gusted to an astonishing two hundred and thirty-one miles per hour. Pagliuca immediately re-checked the arithmetic, while Wendell Lees ran a secondary stopwatch timing. The calculations were verified: humanity had just recorded the fastest surface wind ever measured on planet Earth. The verified two-hundred-and-thirty-one-mile-per-hour gust exerted over one hundred and fifty pounds of pressure per square foot, a colossal aerodynamic force capable of ripping steel roofs from masonry buildings.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: VERIFICATION AND SCIENTIFIC TRIUMPH
Recognizing that such an astronomical figure would be greeted with intense skepticism by the global scientific community, the young meteorologists handled their data with meticulous scientific rigor. Alexander McKenzie immediately coded a radio message to Dr. Charles F. Brooks, director of the Blue Hill Meteorological Observatory in Milton, Massachusetts, reporting the record-shattering two-hundred-and-thirty-one-mile-per-hour measurement.
Dr. Brooks, initially astonished, immediately ordered that the chronograph charts be preserved under seal. When weather permitted days later, the entire anemometer assembly was carefully dismantled from the mast and transported by hand down the cog railway to Massachusetts. The instrument was placed into the wind tunnel at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where aeronautical engineers subjected it to rigorous multi-point calibrations across extreme velocity ranges.
The findings were unequivocal: the calibration tests proved that if anything, the instrument had slightly under-recorded the gust due to rotational inertia, and the true velocity may have been as high as two hundred and thirty-nine miles per hour. The official reading of two hundred and thirty-one miles per hour was certified by the United States Weather Bureau, earning global headlines from The New York Times to the London Times and establishing Mount Washington as the undisputed pinnacle of extreme atmospheric phenomena. The MIT wind tunnel verification proved that the young observers had adhered to the highest standards of empirical scientific rigor under life-threatening sub-zero laboratory conditions.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY OF MOUNT WASHINGTON
The extraordinary world record established on April twelfth, nineteen thirty-four stood unbroken for more than six decades. It was not until May nineteen ninety-six—sixty-two years later—that an unmanned robotic weather station on Barrow Island off the coast of Western Australia recorded a wind gust of two hundred and fifty-three miles per hour during the landfall of Tropical Cyclone Olivia.
Yet Mount Washington's achievement remains unique in the annals of science. Unlike the Barrow Island measurement, which was recorded automatically by an unmanned electronic probe in a hurricane, the Mount Washington record was manually recorded, verified, and defended in person by three brave young scientists who risked their lives in the freezing gales to keep the instruments running.
Today, the non-profit Mount Washington Observatory continues to operate twenty-four hours a day, three hundred and sixty-five days a year, from a modern, steel-reinforced concrete bunker anchored to the summit. Observers still venture outside in sub-zero blizzards to measure temperatures, study rime icing, and test advanced cold-weather gear for NASA and polar expeditions. The historic chronograph chart from April twelfth, nineteen thirty-four remains carefully preserved, a sacred relic of meteorology honoring the day human curiosity stood face-to-face with the greatest wind on Earth. The Mount Washington Observatory remains an enduring beacon of independent American scientific discovery, continuously manned by brave men and women who dare to live where nature is wildest.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Mount Washington's record-shattering two-hundred-and-thirty-one-mile-per-hour wind stood unbroken for over sixty years, a legendary triumph of human bravery and empirical science. I'm Rebecca.
